items.label: A
items.critique: Witty, characterful and socially observant (soldiers left, travellers right; 'How refreshing'). Nox's shopkeepers rarely build a little scene of the town's politics into a greeting; this is a later, more literary register.

items.label: B
items.critique: Flat, generic, slightly awkward lines ('Your money is still good with me') with no place detail at all. That blandness and missing comma are very much Westwood's filler barks.

items.label: C
items.critique: 'Fresher'n a monkey's butt' is the campaign's crude slapstick, and 'Welcome, Wanderer! ... finest wares in all of Nox!' is stock Westwood hype with exclamation marks.

items.label: D
items.critique: Each line is built around a local economic detail (north gate shut, prices climbing, eel stew) plus a punchline ('Mostly.'). Competent, but the ellipsis lists and the world-building in every greeting are the giveaways.

items.label: E
items.critique: Too crafted: the beam joke, a price per bowl, 'Picks are for digging', 'that's no small thing this deep'. Every shop restates the setting (under the mountain), which Westwood never bothered to do.

items.label: F
items.critique: The fish-only menu joke is nice, but again every line carries setting and a rumour hook (boats going missing). The dry deadpan reads modern rather than Nox's broad cheer.

items.label: G
items.critique: Named establishments, 'sir [Class]', a slightly clumsy rivalry jab at another innkeeper, and 'How can I help you?'. Plain, a bit stiff, typical Westwood.

items.label: H
items.critique: 'Welcome to [Person]'s!', the hyphenated punning shop name and 'one stop shop for all your literary needs' are Westwood's ad-copy puns.

items.label: I
items.critique: Lively ('Shut the door! Shut it! ...There.') but each line is a crafted vignette with weather, prices and wit ('I have three', 'Warm one, four gold?'). Too consistent and too clever to be Nox's shop barks.

items.label: J
items.critique: 'aye mate?', 'Ya need some new weapons and armor?' and an expository magic-shop line about a guild supplying a class: the odd, uneven dialect and tone switching are Westwood's.

tells: Westwood's shop greetings are generic and interchangeable: welcome, the shop's name, 'How can I help you?'. The new ones put the local setting (weather, depth, fish, a shut gate) into every line.
The new texts quote concrete prices and stock lists with ellipses ('Swords, shields, mail...'); Westwood rarely names a price in a greeting.

Westwood's humour is broad and crude or pun-based (monkey's butt, punning shop names, 'all your literary needs'); the new humour is dry and observational, with a deadpan turn ('Mostly.', 'I have three').
Westwood's three lines in a set are uneven in tone and quality, sometimes clumsy or missing commas; the new sets are polished and match each other in voice.
Westwood uses forms of address ('Wanderer', 'sir [Class]', 'lad', 'mate') plus exclamation marks; the new texts use more full stops and rhetorical questions.
